newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr dumped, dismayed by RBA haste.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr dumped, dismayed by RBA haste.

text.p: The Australian dollar was hanging by its fingertips late Wednesday after an interest rate cut came like a bolt from the blue to topple it from 80 cents.

To many the 0.5 point easing smacked of indecent haste given the Reserve Bank had only moved five weeks ago and suggested the bank was going all out for growth so yet another could be in store. A stunned local market lopped a cent off the dollar, but left offshore investors to deliver the coup de grace.
It's hard to see the AUD hanging on here," said Chase forex dealer Andrew McGill. "We should take a look lower tonight."
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the dollar had lodged at US$0.7915/20 having been swept from an early US$0.8015.20 and US$0.8020/25 late here Tuesday.
On the crosses it crumbled to 89.60/70 yen from 91.09/19 on Tuesday and its trade weighted index sank to 58.8 from 59.6.

The market had given up on a cut after the RBA's monthly board meeting came and went last week with no news, so was caught completely unawares when the bank announced the easing at its morning market operation. The cut was the third since the cycle began in late July and left official cash rates at 6.0 percent, their lowest level in 2-1/2 years.
Such was the surprise the dollar was frozen at US$0.8020 for almost three minutes after the cut announcement and then gapped to US$0.7960 in one move.
From there it hurried to a 79 cent low before exporters and corporates came bidding for some much-needed forex cover.
Dealers doubted offshore investors would be so sanguine.

"U.S., European, Japanese funds are all long Aussie and have a need to sell," said McGill, a senior dealer on the forex sales desk at Chase Manhattan. "I think we'll have a hard look at US$0.7850 support tonight and, if that gives way, the early November lows around US$0.7815."
The US$0.7810/15 was a pivotal chart area which marked the low point for the dollar after the last rate cut on November 6.

Whether it tested that could well depend on how the market assessed the risk for another policy easing. Opinion was divided on the need for further relaxation, but given the bank had been so aggressive this time few would rule it out.

"Given this early action by the bank, we expect inflationary and growth trends over the next few months to confirm there is scope for a further and final easing of 0.5 point in February or March," said Bill Evans, chief economist at Westpac.
That would take rates close to the 1993 low of 4.75 percent.
The three rate cuts, and the threat of more, had seen the dollar's fat interest differential slimmed down sharply particularly against the U.S. dollar.

Yields on domestic three year bonds, the time period that tended to appeal most to Japanese investors, had fallen about 27 basis points today to 6.42 percent which was only half a point above the comparable U.S. bond.

And dealers also felt the RBA had booby-trapped the dollar by linking its strength to today's easing. "In effect the bank is saying that if the dollar goes back above 80 cents they'll be thinking about another cut," said a wary trader here.
Human nature could also play a part in this process.
"The cut has really taken the steam out of people," he said. "They don't mind when a move has been well flagged, but this sort of shock upsets investors and creates an air of panic."

The RBA's surprise package rendered today's domestic data largely irrelevant, although a sharp 6.7 percent fall in the Westpac consumer sentiment index for December suggested it had been a timely delivery.
Housing finance fell 5.8 percent in October, but the detail was stronger with commitments for new construction up a healthy 13.2 percent. -- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
